_note: Simplified 'Kid mode' steps for early readers. Keyed by lesson title, normalised to lowercase. course.html overlays these when Kid mode is on; Read-to-me reads them aloud. Steps are friendly and explain the why in simple words. Younger tracks read playfully; the teen (13-16) lessons are kept plain but not babyish.

traffic light simulation.intro: Let's build a real traffic light! It will blink red, then green, then yellow — all by itself. 🚦

steps.text: The Arduino is the brain. Keep it unplugged while you build so nothing gets hot.
Put the breadboard flat. The holes in each short row are joined inside, like a secret tunnel.
Look at each LED: one leg is LONG and one is SHORT. Long = plus (+), short = minus (−). Remember that!
Push the red LED in so its two legs sit in two different rows. Do the same for yellow and green, with a gap between.
For each LED, put one end of a 220 Ω resistor in the SAME row as the SHORT leg, and the other end in the blue (−) rail.
Run a black wire from the blue (−) rail to the Arduino's GND hole.
Now the colour wires (look at the diagram!): red LED's LONG-leg row → pin 13, yellow → pin 12, green → pin 11.
Check your board against the wiring diagram. Same pins? Resistors on the short-leg side? Great.
Plug the Arduino into the computer with the USB cable.
Open our code, copy it in, and press the arrow to send it to the board.
Watch! Red waits… green go… quick yellow… then red again, forever.
A light won't turn on? It's probably backwards — swap its legs so the long leg goes to the pin side.
You built a real traffic light. High five! 🙌

prompting power.intro: AI chatbots like ChatGPT can help with almost anything — but only if you ask in a smart way. Let’s learn the secret! 🤖

steps.text: AI chatbots can help with almost anything — but only if you ask in a smart way. Let's learn how!
Sit with a grown-up and open ChatGPT (chat.openai.com), or Copilot, or Gemini.
First, ask a LAZY question. Type exactly: Tell me about dogs. Read the answer.
Notice it's long and a bit boring. The question was fuzzy, so the answer is fuzzy.
Here's the magic recipe — 4 parts: ROLE (who the AI pretends to be), TASK (what you want), DETAIL (who it's for, any limits), FORMAT (a list, story, or table).
Try the recipe: You are a vet. Explain to a curious 8-year-old why dogs wag their tails, in 3 fun facts with emojis.
Compare the two answers side by side. The smart one is much better — same AI, better question!
Now pick something YOU love. Write a lazy version first, then a smart version using all 4 parts. Run both.
Make it even better: add one more rule, like keep it under 50 words or make it funny.
Stay safe: never type your real full name, home address, or school into the chat.
Write your best question on a Recipe Card (Role / Task / Detail / Format) so you can use it again.
You can talk to an AI like a pro now!

ai art studio.intro: Today you're an AI art director — you'll make pictures just by typing words! 🎨

steps.text: An AI art tool turns your words into a picture. The words you type are called a prompt — you're the art director!
Open an AI art tool with a grown-up: Bing Image Creator (bing.com/create) or Craiyon (craiyon.com).
Try a simple prompt: A red bicycle under a mango tree. Press make and watch it draw.
Look closely. What did it get right? What looks funny or wrong? AI isn't perfect!
Now add detail to the SAME idea: watercolour painting, warm afternoon light. Make it again.
Put the two pictures side by side. More detail in = a better picture out.
Change just one word (the colour, the time of day) and see how the art changes.
Save each prompt with its picture so you can see how your words shaped the art.
Free tools only give a few tries, so plan your words before you click.
Think: who's the real artist here — you or the computer? (No easy answer!)
Make a little gallery of your best 3 artworks. You drew with words!

ai music & sound.intro: Today you'll make real music with AI — just by describing it! 🎵

steps.text: An AI music tool has listened to thousands of songs and learned which sounds go together. You just describe what you want!
Grab headphones and open a tool with a grown-up: Soundraw (soundraw.io) or Boomy (boomy.com).
Type a simple brief: upbeat, hopeful, hip-hop, 30 seconds. Press make and play it.
Now score a scene — maybe battle music for a game, or a calm walk through Nairobi.
Didn't love it? Change ONE word, like the mood or the speed, and make it again.
Compare your two tracks. Hear how one word changed the whole feeling?
Each track takes about a minute, so use the wait to plan the next one.
Give your favourite a title and a job, like music for my video.
Think about it: who owns a song a machine helped make? There's no easy answer!
You made your very own AI song. Composer!

ai storytelling.intro: You're an author AND illustrator — and AI is your helper. 📖

steps.text: You're the author AND director. AI is your helper — but YOU make every choice.
Plan first. Fill in four boxes: Character, Setting, Problem, Ending.
Open a text AI (ChatGPT, chat.openai.com) and ask it to draft your story from your 4 boxes.
You're the boss and the editor. Keep what you like, rewrite what you don't.
Open an image AI and describe your main character. The clearer your words, the better the picture.
Draw your settings too. Make a picture for each important moment.
Shape it into a beginning, a middle and an end — about 3 to 6 pages.
Put the words and pictures together in Canva (canva.com) or on paper as a little booklet.
Keep it safe: don't put your real full name or school into the AI.
Read your illustrated story out loud. You directed the whole thing!

teachable machine.intro: Today you'll train your own AI to recognise things — with no code at all! 🧠

steps.text: You'll train your own AI with NO code — just by showing it examples. That's how machines learn!
Open teachablemachine.withgoogle.com with a grown-up and choose Image Project.
Make two classes, like Thumbs Up and Thumbs Down. Give each one LOTS of example photos (30+).
Big idea: AI learns from examples. More fair examples = a smarter model.
Click Train. The AI studies your photos and learns the difference between your classes.
Test it live with your webcam. Hold up a thumbs up — does it guess right?
Try to trick it. When it's wrong, ask: did I give it enough fair examples?
Add more photos for the class it gets wrong, then train again. Testing makes it better.
Remember: an AI is only as good as its data. Unfair examples make an unfair model.
Export your model before you close the tab, or it's gone!
You built a real machine-learning model. Awesome!

mashup madness.intro: You're the AI director, joining several AI tools into one cool project! 🎬

steps.text: You're the director of an AI film crew. Each tool is a specialist — you join them into one project!
Pick a brief, like a poster for a made-up product, or a one-page story.
Station 1 — Text AI: ask a chatbot (ChatGPT) to write the words or script.
Station 2 — Image AI: give those words to an image tool (Bing Image Creator) to make a picture.
Station 3 — Voice AI: use a text-to-speech tool (TTSMaker, ttsmaker.com) to read it aloud.
Station 4 — Assemble: stitch picture, words and voice together in Canva or Google Slides.
A good prompt at each station helps the next one. One weak link and the whole thing wobbles.
Each tool has free limits, so write your best prompt the first time.
Watch your mashup. Fix the weakest station and run it again.
Show off your finished AI mashup!

bias detective.intro: You're a bias detective! AI can give unfair or stereotyped results — let's catch it. 🕵️

steps.text: You're a bias detective! AI learns from its data — if the data is unfair, the AI is unfair too.
Make a report table: Tool · Prompt · What I expected · What I got · Bias spotted.
Ask an image AI for a doctor, then a nurse, then a boss. Save every result.
Try a chatbot and a translator too, with prompts that might reveal a stereotype.
Collect at least 4 pieces of evidence — screenshots or copied text.
Why does it happen? When training data over-shows one group and leaves others out, the AI copies that.
Spot the patterns. For each one, write down what might have caused it.
The goal isn't to distrust AI — it's to use it wisely. What AI shows isn't always true.
Write one real idea for how a fairer tool would collect better data.
Finish your Bias Report. Great detective work!

ai careers deep dive.intro: Meet three real AI jobs and find out what they actually do all day. 💼

steps.text: Building AI takes a team of three. Meet them and find out what each one does all day.
Data Scientist finds & cleans the data. ML Engineer builds the model. AI Ethicist checks it's fair & safe.
Use a chatbot (ChatGPT) as a virtual interviewee. Ask it to role-play each of the three jobs.
Run three mini-interviews. Ask each: what do you do all day, and what tools do you use?
Take notes on each one's answers.
Draw a pipeline showing how all three work on ONE real project.
Spot where they clash — like speed versus fairness. Who wins, and why?
See why good data and ethics matter just as much as the coding.
Explain how the three roles work together to build AI you can trust.
You can now name three AI careers. Nice work!

build your portfolio.intro: Turn something you've built into a professional portfolio piece you can share. 🚀

steps.text: Turn something you built into a portfolio piece anyone can see. This is about showing your work, not new coding.
Pick your best project — the one you're proudest of.
Open or make a free GitHub account at github.com.
Upload your project with a clear README: what it does, why you made it, how it works.
Build a short pitch deck in Gamma (gamma.app) or Google Slides for non-techie people.
Write and rehearse a 2-minute showcase pitch about your project.
A chatbot (ChatGPT or Claude) can help you draft your README and your pitch script.
Set up accounts early — sign-ups and email checks eat your time.
Finish with a live GitHub link and a polished deck you can send to anyone.
You're ready to show your work to the world. Go you!

how ai systems work.intro: Every AI, however clever, is built from three simple parts. Let's see them! 🔍

steps.text: Every AI, however clever, is built from three simple parts. Let's find them!
Draw it big on paper: INPUT → AI SYSTEM → OUTPUT.
Work one out loud: a reminder app. Input = your dates. AI = it checks the calendar. Output = a reminder pops up.
Pick 3 AI tools you really use. On sticky notes, label each one's input, process and output.
Swap with a friend. Does every example have all three parts?
Add a 4th box: FEEDBACK. When you tap 👍, that becomes new input the AI learns from.
A person always decides what goes in and what comes out — AI isn't magic.
Now you can see inside any AI tool!

good data, bad data.intro: AI learns from data — so bad data in means bad answers out! 📊

steps.text: AI learns from data — so bad data in means bad answers out. Let's prove it!
Survey everyone you can — like What's your favourite fruit? — and tally every answer.
That's your GOOD dataset: everyone got a say, so it's fair.
Check it: did anyone get missed? Is a group over- or under-counted?
Now break it on purpose: pretend you only asked the front two rows. Re-tally.
Compare the two answers. See how the broken survey gives a different, unfair result?
If this unfair survey trained an AI, what wrong thing would it learn?
Real example: face-unlock trained on one skin tone works badly for everyone else.
Write 3 rules for collecting fairer, more complete data.
Always ask the big question: who is missing?
Now you know why fair data matters so much!

ethical ai design.intro: Ethics asks not just what an AI CAN do, but what it SHOULD do. ⚖️

steps.text: Ethics asks not just what an AI CAN do, but what it SHOULD do. You're the designer!
Learn the 4 checks every AI should pass: Fairness, Privacy, Safety, and being Explainable (clear).
Pick a product idea — like a face-scanning school gate, or a homework-grading bot.
Fairness & Privacy: who could it treat unfairly? What private data does it collect?
Safety: where is that data stored, and who can see it?
Explainable: how would someone appeal a wrong decision? Add a human check.
Redesign it to pass every check — or drop a risky feature entirely.
Give a 60-second ethics review of your before and after.
There's rarely one right answer — a well-argued trade-off beats a tidy one.
You designed an AI you'd be proud to ship!

explain ai to others.intro: If you can explain AI simply, in plain words, you really understand it. 🗣️

steps.text: If you can explain AI simply, with no fancy words, you really understand it.
Pick one person to explain it to — a parent, a little sibling, or a head teacher.
Ban the jargon: no algorithm, model, or neural network allowed!
Write what AI is in just 3 short sentences, in plain words.
A clear example: AI is a computer that learns from lots of examples, so it can make good guesses about new things.
Say it to a partner. Can they repeat it back in their own words?
Rewrite your weakest sentence using their feedback.
Give your final version to your real listener.
Prove it worked: have THEM explain the idea back to you.
Short and clear beats long and impressive, every time!

button controlled led.intro: Today a button turns a light on and off — like a real wall switch! 🔘

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
LED legs: long = plus (+), short = minus (−).
Push the LED into the breadboard with its legs in two different rows.
Put a 220 Ω resistor from the LED's long-leg row to an empty row, then wire that row to pin 8. (See the diagram.)
Run the LED's short leg to the blue (−) rail, and the rail to the Arduino's GND.
Push the button across the middle gap of the breadboard so its two sides aren't joined.
Wire one button leg to pin 2. Wire the other leg on that side to GND (through the 10 kΩ resistor).
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Press the button — the light turns ON and stays on. Press again — OFF.
Nothing happens? Check the LED isn't backwards and the button straddles the centre gap.
You built a real push-button switch!

fade an led.intro: Today your light will fade in and out smoothly, not just blink. 🌙

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
LED legs: long = plus (+), short = minus (−).
Fading needs a PWM pin — one with a ~ next to the number. We use pin 9.
Push the LED into the breadboard, legs in two rows.
Put a 220 Ω resistor from the short-leg row to the blue (−) rail, and run the rail to Arduino GND.
Run a wire from the LED's long-leg row to pin 9 (~). (See the diagram.)
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Watch the light breathe — slowly brighter, then dimmer, forever.
The code counts from 0 to 255 to set the brightness. Try changing the numbers!
Just on/off, not fading? Make sure it's pin 9 with the ~ symbol.
You made a glowing, fading light!

rgb led colour mixer.intro: Today you'll mix your own colours with light, just like a TV screen does! 🌈

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
An RGB LED is 3 lights in one. Its LONGEST leg is the shared minus (−).
Push the RGB LED in. Run its longest leg to the blue (−) rail, and the rail to GND.
Give each colour leg its own 220 Ω resistor, then wire: Red → pin 9, Green → pin 10, Blue → pin 11. (See the diagram.)
Each knob has 3 legs: one outer → 5V, the other outer → GND, the middle → an analog pin.
Wire the knob middles to A0 (red), A1 (green), A2 (blue).
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Turn the knobs to mix your own colours — red + blue makes purple!
A colour missing? Check that colour's resistor and its pin.
You're mixing millions of colours with light!

capacitive touch sensor.intro: Today a light turns on when you just TOUCH a pad — no button to press! ✋

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
LED legs: long = plus (+), short = minus (−).
Put the LED in. Long leg → 220 Ω resistor → a row wired to pin 8. Short leg → (−) rail → Arduino GND.
The touch sensor (TTP223) has 3 pins: VCC, GND, OUT.
Wire sensor VCC → 5V, GND → GND, OUT → pin 2. (See the diagram.)
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Touch the pad — the light flips on. Touch again — off!
No response? Re-check OUT → pin 2 and VCC → 5V.
You made a magic touch switch!

buzzer melody.intro: Today you make a tiny speaker play a real tune! 🎶

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
Find the buzzer's + leg (it's longer, or marked with a +).
Wire the + leg to pin 8 and the − leg to GND. (See the diagram.) A 100 Ω resistor in between is optional and softens the volume.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Listen — it plays a tune like Ode to Joy!
The code is a list of notes and how long each lasts. Change them to make your own song.
No sound? Make sure it's a passive buzzer and the + leg is on pin 8.
You built a little music machine!

morse code blinker.intro: Today your light sends secret messages in Morse code! 🔦

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
LED legs: long = plus (+), short = minus (−).
Put the LED in. Long leg → 220 Ω resistor → a row wired to pin 9. Short leg → Arduino GND. (See the diagram.)
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Watch the light flash: short = dot, long = dash, with gaps between.
S is dot-dot-dot, O is dash-dash-dash — that spells SOS!
Change the message in the code to send your own secret word.
Not blinking? Check the long leg → pin 9 through the resistor.
You're a Morse code messenger!

temperature logger.intro: Today you build a tiny weather sensor that reads the temperature! 🌡️

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
The DHT11 has 3 pins: VCC (+), GND (−), and DATA.
Wire VCC → 5V, GND → GND, DATA → pin 2. (See the diagram.)
Plug in the USB cable, upload the code, then open the Serial Monitor.
Watch the temperature appear, like 24 °C!
Breathe on the sensor — the number goes up.
Says "no reading"? Check DATA → pin 2 and that the DHT library is installed.
You built a real thermometer!

ultrasonic distance sensor.intro: Today your sensor measures distance using sound — just like a bat! 📏

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
The HC-SR04 has 4 pins: VCC, Trig, Echo, GND.
Wire VCC → 5V, GND → GND, Trig → pin 9, Echo → pin 10. (See the diagram.)
Add the warning LED: long leg → 220 Ω → pin 7, short leg → GND.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Move your hand closer — when it's near, the light warns you!
Check it with a ruler. How close does the warning start?
Always warning? Swap Trig and Echo if they got mixed up.
You built a distance detector!

servo motor control.intro: Today you steer a motor to any angle just by turning a knob! 🤖

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
The knob has 3 legs: one outer → 5V, the other outer → GND, the middle → A0.
The servo has 3 wires: red → 5V, brown/black → GND, orange/yellow → pin 9.
Wire them as in the diagram, and make sure the knob and servo share the same GND.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Turn the knob — the servo arm follows your hand!
Servo jitters? Double-check the shared GND.
You controlled a real motor!

light-activated led.intro: Today your light turns itself ON when it gets dark — like a streetlight! 💡

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
The LDR lets more electricity through in bright light and less in the dark.
Build a divider: one LDR leg → 5V; the other LDR leg shares a row with a 10 kΩ resistor that goes to GND.
From the junction where they meet, run a wire to A0. (See the diagram.)
Add the LED: long leg → 220 Ω → pin 8, short leg → GND.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Cover the sensor with your hand — the light switches on!
Backwards (on in the light)? Swap the LDR and 10 kΩ, or change the threshold number in the code.
You made an automatic night light!

digital dice.intro: Today you build an electronic dice made of lights! 🎲

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
7 LEDs make the dice dots. Give each one a 220 Ω resistor on its SHORT leg down to the (−) rail, then the rail to GND.
Wire the 7 LONG legs to pins 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. (See the diagram.)
Add the roll button: one leg → pin 9, the other → GND.
Leave pin A0 empty — the code uses its random "noise" to shuffle the roll.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Press the button — the lights tumble, then show your roll!
A dot missing? Check that LED's pin and that it isn't backwards.
You built a glowing dice!

basic alarm system.intro: Today you build an alarm that catches movement! 🚨

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
The PIR motion sensor has 3 pins: VCC, OUT, GND.
Wire PIR VCC → 5V, GND → GND, OUT → pin 2. (See the diagram.)
Red LED: long leg → 220 Ω → pin 8, short leg → GND. Wire the Green LED to pin 9 the same way.
Wire the buzzer's + leg → pin 7 and its − leg → GND.
Add the arm button: one leg → pin 4, the other leg → GND through a 10 kΩ resistor.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Press the button to arm (green). Wave your hand — red light and buzzer go off!
Always alarming? Give the PIR about 30 seconds to settle after power-on.
You built a working security alarm!

fan control.intro: Today a sensor turns a fan on all by itself when it gets too hot. 🌡️

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build — and don't connect the 12V yet.
The TMP36 has 3 legs: VCC (5V), OUT (middle), GND. Check the flat face for the order.
Wire VCC → 5V, GND → GND, OUT → A0. (See the diagram.)
Status LED: long leg → 220 Ω → pin 6, short leg → GND.
The relay module has VCC, GND, IN. Wire VCC → 5V, GND → GND, IN → pin 7.
On the relay's big terminals (COM/NO), connect the fan and the 12V supply. This is a SEPARATE circuit — never the Arduino.
Plug in the USB cable, upload the code, THEN connect the 12V.
Warm the sensor — the relay clicks and the fan spins!
Fan never stops? Lower the temperature threshold in the code.
You built an automatic cooling system!

simon says game.intro: Today you build the classic Simon memory game! 🎮

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
Wire Arduino 5V to the red (+) rail and GND to the blue (−) rail.
Each LED: long leg → 220 Ω → a pin (Red 2, Green 3, Yellow 4, Blue 5); short leg → the (−) rail. (See the diagram.)
Each button: one leg → 5V, the other leg → a pin (8, 9, 10, 11) AND through a 10 kΩ resistor to GND.
Buzzer: + leg → pin 12, − leg → GND.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Watch the pattern, then copy it. Each round adds one more colour!
A button does nothing? Check its pin and its 10 kΩ to GND.
You built a real electronic game!

line-following robot.intro: Today you build a robot that drives itself along a line! 🤖

steps.text: Build the chassis first: attach the motors, the wheels and the support ball.
Wire the left motor to the L298N's OUT1/OUT2 and the right motor to OUT3/OUT4.
Wire the L298N to the Arduino: ENA→5, IN1→8, IN2→9, IN3→10, IN4→11, ENB→6. (See the diagram.)
Connect the L298N GND to the Arduino GND — this shared ground is essential.
Connect the battery to the L298N's 12V/GND. Keep its switch OFF for now.
Wire the 2 IR sensors: VCC→5V, GND→GND, left OUT→pin 2, right OUT→pin 3.
Make a track with black tape on a white floor.
Upload the code, then switch the battery on and set the robot on the line.
Motors silent? Check the shared GND and the battery switch.
Your robot follows the track all by itself!

mini smart city.intro: Today you build a mini smart city — 3 systems on one Arduino! 🏙️

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build. Lots of parts here — go slow and tick each off the diagram.
Traffic LEDs (each via a 220 Ω to GND): red → 13, yellow → 12, green → 11.
Street-light LED → 10. Parking LEDs: free → 7, full → 6 (each via a 220 Ω to GND).
HC-SR04: VCC→5V, GND→GND, Trig→9, Echo→8.
LDR divider (with a 10 kΩ) into A0, just like the night-light project.
Wire the LCD: RS→2, EN→3, D4→4, D5→5, D6→A1, D7→A2, plus its contrast knob. (See the diagram.)
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Watch it all run at once: traffic cycling, street light on in the dark, parking showing FREE/FULL.
LCD blank? Turn the contrast knob until the text appears.
You built a working model city!

obstacle-avoiding robot.intro: Today you build a robot that drives around without bumping into things! 🤖

steps.text: Build the chassis and mount the L298N on top.
Left motor → OUT1/OUT2, right motor → OUT3/OUT4.
Wire the L298N to the Arduino: IN1→8, IN2→9, IN3→10, IN4→11, ENA→5, ENB→6. (See the diagram.)
L298N GND → Arduino GND (shared ground is essential).
Battery → L298N 12V/GND — never the Arduino's 5V pin.
Mount the servo and sensor. Servo: red→5V, brown→GND, signal→pin 3.
HC-SR04: VCC→5V, GND→GND, Trig→12, Echo→13.
Upload the code and switch the battery on.
Put a box in its path — it stops, looks left and right, then turns away!
Acting strange? Check that ALL the grounds are joined together.
You built a robot that thinks for itself!

weather station.intro: Today you build a weather station that shows temperature and humidity on a screen! 🌦️

steps.text: Keep the Arduino unplugged while you build.
The DHT11 has 3 pins: + (VCC), out (data), − (GND).
Wire VCC → 5V, GND → GND, data → pin 2. (See the diagram.)
The LCD's I2C backpack has 4 pins: VCC, GND, SDA, SCL.
Wire VCC → 5V, GND → GND, SDA → A4, SCL → A5.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Watch live readings like "24°C 60%" appear on the screen!
Blank screen? Try the other I2C address in the code (0x27 or 0x3F).
You built your own weather station!

voice- / gesture-controlled robot.intro: Today AI meets robot — you'll drive a robot with your gestures or your voice! 🧠

steps.text: First, train your AI on Teachable Machine (in Chrome) with gesture or voice examples.
Build the robot: Arduino, L298N, 2 motors + wheels, chassis, battery.
Left motor → OUT1/OUT2, right motor → OUT3/OUT4.
Wire the L298N to the Arduino: ENA→5, IN1→8, IN2→9, ENB→6, IN3→10, IN4→11. (See the diagram.)
L298N GND → Arduino GND. Battery → L298N 12V/GND.
Upload the robot code, then close the Serial Monitor.
Open your Teachable Machine page in Chrome and connect it to the Arduino over USB.
Point left — the robot turns left! Say "stop" — it stops!
"No port" in Chrome? Close the Arduino Serial Monitor first — Chrome needs the port.
You built an AI-powered robot — amazing!

robot arm basics.intro: Today you build a cardboard robot arm and steer it with knobs! 🦾

steps.text: Build the cardboard arm: a base, two bones, and gripper jaws. A grown-up does the knife cutting.
Fit the 4 servos at the joints: base, shoulder, elbow and gripper.
Wire each servo's signal wire: base → 3, shoulder → 5, elbow → 6, gripper → 9. (See the diagram.)
Power the servos from their OWN battery/5V — not the Arduino's 5V pin.
Join the battery's GND to the Arduino's GND so they share a ground.
Each knob: one outer leg → 5V, the other → GND, the middle → A0, A1, A2, A3.
Plug in the USB cable and upload the code.
Turn the 4 knobs to move the arm live — lift, bend, and grab!
Servos jitter or the board resets? They're pulling too much power — use the separate 5V battery.
You built your own robot arm!
